summary: Long technical deep dive focused on private VPC and hybrid on-prem connectivity to Redwood Private. Key topics: control plane connectivity (outbound-only), PrivateLink vs interface endpoints, NAT and egress design, subnet sizing and ENI limits, DNS (split-horizon) and mTLS for control plane, runtime impacts on latency from KV cache location and batching/quantization tradeoffs. Agreed next steps include diagrams, perf checklist, and security docs.
topics: Control plane egress and PrivateLink alternatives
NAT, subnets, ENI and MTU considerations
DNS resolution & split-horizon for internal hostnames
Runtime perf: KV cache placement, batching, quantization
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Alright everyone, thanks for making time. We're gonna run through the private VPC + on-prem networking integration and then Lucas will walk perf knobs.
[00:18] Alex (BlueStream): thanks, we have the infra folks and security here, want to make sure the control plane and data plane remain private, and we avoid wide open egress.
[00:32] Lucas (SE): Quick agenda: control plane connectivity, PrivateLink vs interface endpoints, NAT/egress patterns, DNS and split-horizon, then runtime specifics - KV caching, batching, quant, and how those affect p50/p95.
[00:49] Rina (App): we also wanna understand if the KV cache can be colocated on-prem or needs to be in the same VPC as the runtime nodes.
[01:05] Lucas: great q. Short answer: the KV cache can be local to the inference cluster to avoid cross-region calls. For Redwood Private we support local ephemeral KV and optional central cache. But if you keep KV on-prem, latency to the model is lower but you need RAM and fast NVMe to store large key-value segments.
[01:32] Samir (Sec): can you clarify control plane flows? we don't want inbound from internet, prefer outbound-only with allowlisted IPs or PrivateLink.
[01:45] Maya: yeah our typical pattern for Private deployments is outbound-only control plane connections to our managed control endpoints, or you can stabilize via interface endpoints and our VPC endpoint service. We also support a private peering model for some enterprises.
[02:03] Diego: just to add, the control plane uses TLS 1.2/1.3 and mTLS for agent registration. For strict environments we recommend interface endpoints + route-table locks.
[02:20] Alex: about PrivateLink - is that a managed service on your side? we ran into account-based endpoint issues before.
[02:32] Maya: we run an AWS endpoint service for PrivateLink; customers create interface endpoints in their VPC and we accept connections. Caveat: cross-account interface endpoints require you to approve the endpoint or we can pre-approve via AWS principals. Alternative is Transit Gateway peering if customers use TGW.
[02:54] Kelly (Platform): what's the difference in performance/latency between PrivateLink and outbound HTTPS to your control plane? is there a big delta?
[03:05] Lucas: PrivateLink avoids NAT and internet hops, so small but consistent improvement in control traffic latency — few tens of ms on registration or small API calls. For heavy data path, it doesn't change token streaming latency unless your runtime proxies through control plane which we do not. Runtime is local to your infra — model inference traffic is within your VPC.
[03:29] Alex: okay. NAT gateways - we try to minimize cost. can we use egress via a central proxy or NAT instance? any gotchas?
[03:40] Lucas: yes central NAT instances are fine. Just watch for SNAT ports and connection churn if you have many ENIs. NAT gateway scales but is pricier. Also watch MTU differences if you're crossing VPN tunnels or Direct Connect - fragmentations can affect throughput for large payloads.
[04:02] Rina: DNS concerns — we do split-horizon for internal hostnames. How do your agents resolve your control hostnames when using PrivateLink vs public?
[04:16] Diego: with interface endpoints you point the hostname to the endpoint ENIs. For outbound public TLS you can use split-horizon DNS to map the control plane FQDN to the private IPs of the endpoint. We provide the A record targets and recommend Route53 inbound resolver or your on-prem DNS forwarders configured with conditional forwarding.
[04:41] Samir: any need for special certs? we use internal PKI.
[04:47] Maya: we support mTLS so our agents can present client certs; we also support CA pinning. For internal PKI you can provide certs to the agent; Redwood will validate during bootstrap. We also integrate with customer KMS for key wrapping if you need HSM-backed keys for model encryption.
[05:10] Alex: network limits — ENI and ephemeral ports — how many pods per node do you recommend for heavy concurrency workloads?
[05:20] Lucas: depends on instance type. For high-concurrency we suggest fewer pods per host if each pod opens many upstream sockets. Also enable connection pooling and reuse; our runtime supports long-lived HTTP/2 and keep-alive. If you expect many short-lived outbound requests, increase ephemeral port range or use NAT with port address translation.
[05:43] Kelly: can you comment on cross-AZ latency—we're multi-AZ and want low p95.
[05:49] Lucas: best to keep inference nodes and KV cache in same AZ for lowest p95. If you need HA across AZs, replicate KV using async replication; expect higher p95 on misses due to cross-AZ fetch. Batching helps amortize latency, but for strict p95 goals prefer local KV.
[06:12] Rina: batching — what's the typical latency tradeoff when you increase batch size from 1 to 8? we care about p50 vs p95.
[06:21] Lucas: simple numbers (very workload dependent): single token latencies might be ~30-50ms; batching to 4 could add 10-30ms scheduling overhead but give 3-4x throughput. At higher batch sizes you may hit memory/kv cache pressure and higher tail latencies. We expose batching policies: max_batch_size, max_wait_ms, and priority lanes.
[06:46] Alex: quantization — will 4-bit quant models change CPU/GPU throughput and did you see accuracy regressions?
[06:54] Diego: 4-bit quant gives significant memory reduction and usually 1.5-2x throughput on GPU for many transformers. Accuracy regression depends on model and task — we run eval sets and offer recommended quant profiles. For hallucination-sensitive tasks avoid aggressive quant at first.
[07:12] Samir: how's the runtime handle cache eviction and hot keys? e.g., peak hours with sudden burst of certain prompts.
[07:22] Lucas: we use an LRU-ish policy plus a hot-key hotlist where frequently accessed KV shards are pinned if you configure pinning. Eviction is async; on misses we stream incremental loads so the runtime doesn't stall entirely. But cold-starts will show higher p95. We advise a warmup pass or pre-populate KV for known prompts.
[07:48] Rina: can we pin only top-10k keys? storage-wise what's the footprint?
[07:53] Lucas: depends on key size; we can give a rough spreadsheet. For 10k keys at ~500 bytes it's ~5MB — but for embeddings and longer contexts it grows.
[08:07] Alex: about on-prem - we plan to run inference in our colo with a firewall. Do you need open ports inbound?
[08:15] Maya: no inbound. The agent will initiate outbound TLS to our control endpoints or to the interface endpoint. For PrivateLink the endpoint sits in your subnet and connects to our service; no inbound open to public internet.
[08:31] Kelly: what's the behavior during network partition? our cluster loses egress intermittently for a few minutes.
[08:38] Diego: runtime can operate in short offline mode if models and KV are local; control plane ops (metrics, telemetry) will queue. If your deployment uses external KMS for keys, runtime will need to reach KMS — we recommend a local KMS proxy or cached DEKs to tolerate transient outages.
[08:59] Alex: we use a KMS in another VPC. Any certified patterns for cross-vpc KMS calls without internet?
[09:07] Lucas: use VPC endpoints for the KMS and S3 if you store artifacts. For cross-account KMS you can set key policy to allow the role, and call through interface endpoints or via Transit Gateway peering with route tables. Avoid NAT egress for KMS where possible.
[09:29] Rina: can you show a sample route table diagram for interface endpoints and private subnets? we wanna see recommended CIDR ranges.
[09:36] Maya: yes, we'll send a diagram. Typical pattern: split private subnets per AZ for runtime, a management subnet with interface endpoints and NAT for bootstrap, and a separate subnet for logs and metrics with S3 endpoints.
[09:55] Alex: curious about MTU - our VPN to colo uses 1400 MTU; does that impact streaming tokens?
[10:02] Diego: fragmentation can add CPU overhead and increase tail latency for large payloads. We recommend testing streaming payloads through your VPN; increase keep-alives and lower batch payload sizes if you see fragmentation.
[10:18] Samir: compliance — we need audit logs, flow logs, and SSO. do you capture request-level traces?
[10:26] Maya: yes, Redwood Console collects token-level cost traces, request IDs, and we can forward logs to your Splunk/Cloudwatch via private pipeline. For Private deployments we ship a forwarding agent that writes to S3 or your SIEM over private endpoints.
[10:44] Rina: let's shift to perf checklist — what configs should we test for first?
[10:50] Lucas: I'd recommend three sweeps: baseline single-worker single-thread; then concurrency with batching (ini batch=4, max_wait_ms=25); then quant model test. Measure p50/p95, token throughput, and RAM/VRAM usage. Also measure cold-start vs warmed KV.
[11:13] Alex: do you have a script or harness to replay traffic to simulate our qps?
[11:18] Diego: yes, we have a replay harness that can run against a local endpoint. Lucas will share steps and config.
[11:27] Maya: quick question from procurement: licensing and offline device use — can we air-gap? how long is the licensing check?
[11:36] Maya (AE, slightly laughing): we can do an air-gapped on-prem package. Some features like auto-update will be manual. Licensing heartbeat can be configured to use your internal license server; or we can do a once-off signed license for stricter air-gapped setups.
[11:52] Alex: any particular kernel or driver versions you require for GPUs when running quantized kernels?
[11:58] Diego: yes, we recommend NVIDIA driver >= 525 and CUDA 12+ for best kernel support, and certain cuBLAS patches. We'll send a compatibility matrix. Also for small LLMs CPU quant libs like Q8_0 require glibc >= 2.28 — oddities we've seen in older distros.
[12:22] Rina: metrics - what should we track to detect KV pressure before it impacts p95?
[12:29] Lucas: track cache hit ratio, cache-eviction rate, prefetch queue depth, and tail-latency per request path. We also expose per-route token latency and backing-store latency.
[12:45] Samir: if we use cross-AZ replication for KV, will write amplification cause increased network egress costs?
[12:53] Lucas: yes, replication increases intra-VPC bandwidth. Async replication reduces write latency impact but increases background bandwidth. There's a cost/latency tradeoff.
[13:07] Alex: got it. Anything else on security hardening?
[13:12] Samir: do you support SAML SSO for Console and RBAC for token generation?
[13:18] Maya: yes SAML + SCIM and granular RBAC. For Private we can integrate with your IdP either via the control plane or an on-prem identity proxy.
[13:28] Kelly: wrapping up — can we recap next steps?
[13:33] Maya: sure. Lucas will deliver perf checklist and sample harness, I'll share network onboarding doc and interface endpoint CF template, Alex will send ASN and TGW details, and we'll reconvene after we've run the baseline perf. Any final quick q?
[13:50] Alex: nope, thanks all.
[13:52] Maya: thanks team. End call.
